bmt-2019-individual-01.title: The polynomial is constant
bmt-2019-individual-01.body:
A non-constant polynomial of degree at most $3$ has no global maximum unless it is a downward-opening parabola, whose maximum is at its vertex. But $p(1)=p(2)$ would put the vertex at $x=\frac32$, not at $1$. Hence $p$ is constant, $p\equiv5$, and $p(10)=5$.

**Answer: 5**

bmt-2019-individual-02.title: Inscribed angle
bmt-2019-individual-02.body:
$B$ is the midpoint of $AC$, and $A$ and $C$ lie on the circle centred at $B$ with radius $\frac13$. Since $PB=PC=BC=\frac13$, triangle $PBC$ is equilateral and $\angle PBC=60^\circ$. In the circle centred at $B$, $\angle PAC$ is an inscribed angle on arc $PC$, whose central angle is $\angle PBC=60^\circ$, so $\angle PAC=30^\circ$.

**Answer: $30$ degrees**

bmt-2019-individual-03.title: Constant function
bmt-2019-individual-03.body:
Setting $x=0$ gives $f(y)=f(0)$ for all real $y$, so $f$ is constant. Since $f(2019)=17$, $f(17)=17$.

**Answer: 17**

bmt-2019-individual-04.title: All three are B-chips
bmt-2019-individual-04.body:
All three chips must be B-chips. Probability $\frac38\cdot\frac27\cdot\frac16=\frac1{56}$.

**Answer: $\frac1{56}$**

bmt-2019-individual-04.title: Count subsets
bmt-2019-individual-04.body:
There are $\binom83=56$ equally likely sets of $3$ chips and exactly $\binom33=1$ consists of only B-chips.

**Answer: $\frac1{56}$**

bmt-2019-individual-05.title: Annulus
bmt-2019-individual-05.body:
Let $F$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to $A$. A line through $P$ meeting $A$ at distance $r$ from $F$ makes angle $\theta$ with the plane where $\tan\theta=\frac{\sqrt3}r$. The condition $30^\circ\le\theta\le60^\circ$ means $1\le r\le3$ (at $30^\circ$, $r=\frac{\sqrt3}{\tan30^\circ}=3$; at $60^\circ$, $r=1$). So $Q$ is the annulus between radii $1$ and $3$, with area $(9-1)\pi=8\pi$.

**Answer: $8\pi$**

bmt-2019-individual-06.title: Surface minus dots
bmt-2019-individual-06.body:
The cube has surface area $6\cdot2^2=24$ square inches. There are $1+2+\dots+6=21$ dots, each of radius $\frac16$ and area $\frac{\pi}{36}$, for a total of $\frac{21\pi}{36}=\frac{7\pi}{12}$. The paint needed is $24-\frac{7\pi}{12}$ square inches.

**Answer: $24-\frac{7\pi}{12}$**

bmt-2019-individual-07.title: Compare areas
bmt-2019-individual-07.body:
Each corner triangle is equilateral with side $m$ (two sides $m$ and a $60^\circ$ angle), with area $\frac{\sqrt3}4m^2$. The three together have area $\frac{3\sqrt3}4m^2$, and the hexagon is what remains: $\frac{\sqrt3}4M^2-\frac{3\sqrt3}4m^2$. Setting these equal gives $M^2=6m^2$, so $\frac mM=\frac1{\sqrt6}=\frac{\sqrt6}6$.

**Answer: $\frac{\sqrt6}6$**

bmt-2019-individual-08.title: Where the rounding changes
bmt-2019-individual-08.body:
$\operatorname{round}\left(\frac n{2019}\right)$ increases by $1$ exactly when $\frac n{2019}$ passes a half-integer $k+\frac12$. Since $\frac{1009}{2019}<\frac12<\frac{1010}{2019}$, this happens exactly at $n=1010+2019k$, so $g_n=1$ exactly for these $n$. In $[1,2019^2]$ these are $k=0,1,\dots,2018$, i.e. $2019$ values. The expected value is $\frac{2019}{2019^2}=\frac1{2019}$.

**Answer: $\frac1{2019}$**

bmt-2019-individual-09.title: Count by length
bmt-2019-individual-09.body:
Use the $26$-letter alphabet. Every $1$-letter string is a palindrome, so there are $0$ almost-palindromes of length $1$. A $2$-letter string is an almost-palindrome iff its letters differ: $26\cdot25=650$. A $3$-letter string $xyz$ is a palindrome iff $x=z$; if $x\ne z$ we can change one of them to make it a palindrome, so all non-palindromes work: $26^3-26^2=16900$. Total: $650+16900=17550$.

**Answer: 17550**

bmt-2019-individual-10.title: Angle chase
bmt-2019-individual-10.body:
Let $\angle BMT=a$. Then $\angle MBA=180^\circ-\angle MBT=180^\circ-3.5a$, and since triangle $MAB$ is right-angled at $A$, $\angle AMB=3.5a-90^\circ$. Because $MT$ is a diagonal, $\angle AMT=45^\circ=\angle AMB+\angle BMT=4.5a-90^\circ$, so $a=30^\circ$ and $\angle AMB=15^\circ$. Then $AB=\tan15^\circ=2-\sqrt3$ and $BT=1-(2-\sqrt3)=\sqrt3-1$. The area of $\triangle BMT$ is $\frac12\cdot BT\cdot MA=\frac{\sqrt3-1}2$.

**Answer: $\frac{\sqrt3-1}2$**

bmt-2019-individual-11.title: Arcs of radius 1 and 2
bmt-2019-individual-11.body:
Each hinge turns the chord through the interior angle of the $17$-gon, $\pi-\frac{2\pi}{17}=\frac{15\pi}{17}$. $P$ is $2$ from $V_2$, so the first arc has radius $2$. After the first hinge the chord is $V_2V_3$ and $P$ is $1$ from $V_3$, so the next arc (around $V_3$) has radius $1$, then radius $2$ around $V_4$, and so on: radii alternate $2,1,2,1,\dots$.

After $17$ hinges the chord is back on $V_1V_2$ but $P$ is $2$ from $V_1$ (the last hinge had radius $2$), not $1$. After $34$ hinges the chord is back with $P$ in its original place. So $P$ traces $17$ arcs of radius $2$ and $17$ arcs of radius $1$, each of angle $\frac{15\pi}{17}$:
$$17\cdot\frac{15\pi}{17}\cdot(2+1)=45\pi.$$

**Answer: $45\pi$**

bmt-2019-individual-12.title: Squares of repunits
bmt-2019-individual-12.body:
The squares of $1,11,111,\dots$ are $1,121,12321,\dots$ with digit sums $1,4,9,\dots,n^2$ up to $n=9$ ($1234567654321$ has digit sum $81$). For $n=10$ the square is $1234567900987654321$, whose digit sum is $82$. Computing the squares for larger $n$, the digit sums are $85$ exactly for $n=11$ ($12345679012320987654321$ has digit sum $85$), and the sums keep growing afterwards, so there is no other solution. (A direct computer check for $n\le29$ confirms only $n=11$.)

**Answer: 11**

bmt-2019-individual-13.title: Two right triangles
bmt-2019-individual-13.body:
Since $\angle CAB=90^\circ$, $BC$ is a diameter of $O_1$; since $\angle ABD=90^\circ$, $AD$ is a diameter of $O_2$. The quadrilateral $CADB$ (with $C$ and $D$ on opposite sides of $AB$) splits along $AB$ into triangles $ABC$ and $ABD$.

In $O_2$ (radius $10$) the chord $AB$ subtends $60^\circ$, so $AB=10$ and, as $AD=20$, $BD=10\sqrt3$. Area $ABD=\frac12\cdot10\cdot10\sqrt3=50\sqrt3$.

In $O_1$ the inscribed angle $\angle ACB$ on chord $AB$ is $\frac{45^\circ}2=22.5^\circ$, so $AC=\frac{AB}{\tan22.5^\circ}=\frac{10}{\sqrt2-1}=10+10\sqrt2$. Area $ABC=\frac12\cdot10\cdot(10+10\sqrt2)=50+50\sqrt2$.

Total: $50+50\sqrt2+50\sqrt3$, so $a=b=c=50$, $k=2$, $\ell=3$ and $a+b+c+k+\ell=155$.

**Answer: 155**

bmt-2019-individual-14.title: Search
bmt-2019-individual-14.body:
We need $100h+m=x^2$ and $60h+m=y^2$ with $0\le m<60$. Subtracting gives $40h=x^2-y^2$, so $x^2-y^2$ must be a multiple of $40$ (and then $h=\frac{x^2-y^2}{40}\le23$). Checking all hours $h=1,\dots,23$ and minutes $0\le m\le59$ gives exactly two times: $01{:}21$ and $20{:}25$. For $20{:}25$: $2025=45^2$ and $20\cdot60+25=1225=35^2$.

**Answer: 20:25**

bmt-2019-individual-15.title: Count by length and number of nonzero digits
bmt-2019-individual-15.body:
The available digits are $0,0,0$ and the five distinct digits $4,7,2,1,9$, each usable once. A number with $t$ digits and $r$ nonzero digits uses an ordered choice of $r$ nonzero digits ($\frac{5!}{(5-r)!}$ ways) and $t-r\le3$ zeros placed anywhere except the first position ($\binom{t-1}{t-r}$ ways).

Totals by length: $t=1$: $5$; $t=2$: $5+20=25$; $t=3$: $5+40+60=105$; $t=4$: $5+60+180+120=365$; $t=5$: $80+360+480+120=1040$; $t=6$: $600+1200+600=2400$; $t=7$: $2400+1800=4200$; $t=8$: $4200$.

Sum: $5+25+105+365+1040+2400+4200+4200=12340$.

**Answer: 12340**

bmt-2019-individual-16.title: Affine reduction
bmt-2019-individual-16.body:
Ratios of areas and parallelism are preserved by affine maps, so take $A=(0,0)$, $B=(1,0)$, $C=(0,1)$ (area $\frac12$) and $O=(u,v)$. The lines are $y=v$ ($\parallel AB$), $x+y=u+v$ ($\parallel BC$) and $x=u$ ($\parallel CA$). They meet the sides in six points, and the hexagon is the triangle minus three corner triangles: at $A$ (area $\frac12uv$), at $B$ (area $\frac12v(1-u-v)$) and at $C$ (area $\frac12u(1-u-v)$).

With $s=u+v$, the removed fraction of the triangle is $uv+s(1-s)\le\frac{s^2}4+s-s^2=s-\frac34s^2\le\frac13$, with equality at $s=\frac23$, $u=v=\frac13$ (the centroid). So the hexagon has at least $\frac23$ of the triangle's area.

Heron: $s=75$, area $=\sqrt{75\cdot49\cdot24\cdot2}=420$. The minimum is $\frac23\cdot420=280$.

**Answer: 280**

bmt-2019-individual-17.title: Coordinates around D
bmt-2019-individual-17.body:
Put $D$ at the origin with $AB$ along the $x$-axis and $EF$ along the $y$-axis, $A=(-t,0)$, $E=(0,\mp t)$ and $O=(p,q)$ with $p^2+q^2=\frac12$. $A$ and $E$ on the unit circle give $(t+p)^2+q^2=1$ and $p^2+(e-q)^2=1$ with $e=\pm t$. Hence $t^2+2pt=\frac12=t^2-2eq$, so $|p|=|q|=\frac12$ and $t^2\pm t=\frac12$. Since $D$ is closer to $A$ than to $B$, $t=\frac{\sqrt3-1}2$, with $O=(\frac12,\frac12)$, $A=(-t,0)$, $E=(0,-t)$.

The region is right triangle $ADE$ plus the circular segment on chord $AE$. $AE=t\sqrt2$, so $\sin\frac\theta2=\frac{t\sqrt2}2=\sin15^\circ$ and the central angle is $\theta=30^\circ$. Segment area $=\frac12(\frac\pi6-\frac12)=\frac\pi{12}-\frac14$; triangle area $=\frac{t^2}2=\frac{2-\sqrt3}4$.

Total $=\frac\pi{12}+\frac{1-\sqrt3}4=\frac{3-3\sqrt3+\pi}{12}$. So $a=3,b=-3,c=3,d=1,e=12$ and $a+b+c+d+e=16$.

**Answer: 16**

bmt-2019-individual-18.title: Longest trail in a graph
bmt-2019-individual-18.body:
Make a graph on the values $\pm2,\dots,\pm6$, joining $x$ and $y$ (loops allowed, $x=y$) when $f(x,y)\ne0$, with edge weight $f(x,y)$. A valid sequence is a trail using each edge at most once, and its score is the total weight of the edges used.

The values $\pm5$ form a separate component of weight $3$, so we use the component of $\pm2,\pm3,\pm4,\pm6$. Its edges: $8$ loops (weight $1$ each), the $4$ edges $x\leftrightarrow-x$ (weight $1$), and the cross edges $(\pm2,\pm4)$ (weight $2$), $(\pm2,\pm6)$ (weight $3$), $(\pm3,\pm6)$ (weight $2$), four of each. Total weight $8+4+4\cdot2+4\cdot3+4\cdot2=40$.

Every one of the $8$ vertices has odd degree (ignoring loops), but a trail can have at most $2$ odd vertices. We must delete edges to fix $6$ of them; the cheapest way is to delete three of the weight-$1$ edges $x\leftrightarrow-x$ (cost $3$), after which an Euler trail exists. The maximum score is $40-3=37$; for example $6,6,3,3,-6,-6,-3,-3,6,6,2,2,4,4,-2,-2,-4,-4,2,2,-6,-6,-2,-2,6$ achieves $37$ (the official solution's sequence).

**Answer: 37**

bmt-2019-individual-19.title: Equioscillation
bmt-2019-individual-19.body:
Try $a=1$, $b=-\frac{\sqrt3}9$: $f(x)=x^3-x+\frac{\sqrt3}9$. Then $f(0)=\frac{\sqrt3}9$, $f(1)=\frac{\sqrt3}9$ and at the critical point $x=\frac1{\sqrt3}$, $f=-\frac{2}{3\sqrt3}+\frac{\sqrt3}9=-\frac{\sqrt3}9$. So $|f|\le\frac{\sqrt3}9$ on $[0,1]$ with the error alternating at $x=0,\frac1{\sqrt3},1$.

This is optimal: define $\ell(g)=\frac12\left[\frac1{\sqrt3}g(1)+\left(1-\frac1{\sqrt3}\right)g(0)-g\left(\tfrac1{\sqrt3}\right)\right]$. The absolute values of the coefficients sum to $1$, so $|\ell(g)|\le\max_{[0,1]}|g|$. And $\ell(ax+b)=0$ for all $a,b$, while $\ell(x^3)=\frac12\left[\frac1{\sqrt3}-\frac1{3\sqrt3}\right]=\frac{\sqrt3}9$. Hence for every $a,b$, $\max|x^3-ax-b|\ge|\ell(x^3-ax-b)|=\frac{\sqrt3}9$, and the minimum is attained at the polynomial above.

Therefore $a+b=1-\frac{\sqrt3}9$.

**Answer: $1-\frac{\sqrt3}9$**

bmt-2019-individual-20.title: Closed form
bmt-2019-individual-20.body:
With $S=\sum_{n\ge1}F_nd^{-n}$ and $F_{n+1}=xF_n+yF_{n-1}$, $S=\frac d{d^2-xd-y}$ (for $d$ larger than the dominant root of $t^2=xt+y$, which holds for the solutions below). So $\frac1{F_k}=S$ becomes $d^2-(x+F_k)d-y=0$, i.e. $d=\frac{m+\sqrt{m^2+4y}}2$ with $m=x+F_k$ (the other root is negative). Hence $d$ is an integer iff $m^2+4y$ is a perfect square, and then $d>m\ge2$, so $d\ge3$.

$d=3$ requires $m=2$ and $m^2+4y=16$, i.e. $x=F_k=1$ and $y=3$. Then $F=1,1,4,7,19,\dots$ and $(x+F_k)^2+12=z^2$ forces $(z-m)(z+m)=12$, so $m=2$ only: the solutions are exactly $(d,k)=(3,1)$ and $(3,2)$. This is exactly two solutions, so the least possible $d$ is $3$.

**Answer: 3**
